{"url": "https://api.crossref.org/works?query=artificial+agency+moral+responsibility+accountability+decision+consequences+attribution&rows=4&select=DOI%2Ctitle%2Cabstract%2CURL%2Cpublished", "scope": "Crossref bibliographic metadata and abstracts where supplied; not full papers", "excerpt": "[{\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7483422\", \"title\": [\"Self-Good Desire and the Moral Agency of Artificial Intelligence :A Criterion of Life Integrity for Responsibility Attribution\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>The increasing autonomy of artificial intelligence has intensified the \\\"responsibility gap\\\" and the debate over AI moral agency. Existing accounts commonly appeal to rational capacity, sentience, or functional performance, but these criteria do not fully explain either the motivational basis for taking norms as reasons or the conditions under which a subject can bear ultimate moral responsibility. Drawing on the framework developed in On Self-Good Desire, this paper argues that \\\"self-good desire\\\" (sishan yuqiu) is a motivationally necessary condition of full moral agency. It denotes an intrinsic, selfnurturing motivational structure through which a living subject maintains its existence, improves its condition, and pursues its development, unfolding into eleven root desires: self-preservation, self-care, self-enrichment, self-beautification, self-joy, self-compassion, self-reflection, self-confidence, selfstrengthening, self-respect, and freedom. \\\"Life integrity\\\" here does not reduce moral agency to a particular biological substrate; rather, it refers to an integrated organization of self-maintenance, felt value, diachronic identity, and self-concern. Self-good desire is not sufficient for full moral agency, which also requires normative understanding, behavioral control, and responsibility-bearing capacity. On this account, current AI systems can represent norms and simulate forms of moral reasoning, yet there is presently insufficient warrant to attribute to them endogenous needs, first-person experience, enduring self-concern, or genuinely self-generated stakes. They therefore should not be treated as full moral agents. When AI systems cause harm, ultimate moral responsibility should ordinarily remain with human and institutional actors and be allocated by reference to control, causal contribution, benefit, foreseeability, and duties of care. The paper also addresses objections concerning infants, animals, corporations, functionalism, biologism, and future artificial agents, while remaining conditionally open to future artificial systems that might develop functionally equivalent forms of endogenous concern.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7483422\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.4324/9781315201399-4\", \"title\": [\"Technologically blurred accountability?\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315201399-4\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2017, 11, 13]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.1007/978-3-032-15112-4_18\", \"title\": [\"Moral Responsibility Without Moral Agency\"], \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-15112-4_18\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}, {\"DOI\": \"10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"title\": [\"Artificial Intelligence and Legal Responsibility: Agency, Causal Attribution, Foreseeability and the Reconstruction of Liability in Autonomous Systems\"], \"abstract\": \"<jats:p>Contemporary liability doctrine addresses artificial intelligence through three analytically separate inquiries: agency doctrine, which asks who authorized an act; causal-attribution doctrine, which asks what produced a harm; and foreseeability doctrine, which asks what a reasonable actor should have anticipated. Each inquiry anchors its analysis to a different moment in a system's lifecycle-delegation, harm, and design, respectively. For conventional tools this temporal separation is harmless because a single human actor typically occupies all three positions at once. Autonomous systems break that coincidence: the interval between design, delegation, and harm now contains machine-generated intervening choices that no human actor directly authorized, observed, or could fully anticipate. This article develops the thesis that recent liability reforms-the European Union's Product Liability Directive (EU) 2024/2853, the United Kingdom's Automated Vehicles Act 2024, the Republic of Korea's Basic Act on the Development of Artificial Intelligence and Establishment of a Foundation for Trust, and Brazil's pending Marco Legal da Inteligência Artificial (PL 2338/2023)-each stabilize only one of these three temporal anchors without reconciling how the anchors interact when a single harm implicates all three simultaneously. Using doctrinal and comparative legal analysis across these four jurisdictions plus United States tort doctrine, the article identifies this structural problem as temporal anchor divergence: the three liability inquiries increasingly point to different responsible parties for the same harm rather than converging on one, and current reforms treat this divergence as an implementation detail rather than a problem requiring an explicit resolution rule. The article's original contribution is the Temporal Anchor Convergence Standard (TACS), a three-part interpretive frameworkanchor declaration, divergence disclosure, and a default convergence-priority rule keyed to informational control over the intervening period-designed to make the divergence visible to courts and regulators rather than resolved silently by whichever doctrine a claimant happens to plead first. The article confronts the principal counterargument, that existing presumption-based reforms already solve the evidentiary problem regardless of which doctrinal anchor is used, and identifies the conditions under which that objection holds and the conditions under which it does not. The analysis is doctrinal and comparative rather than empirical, and its conclusions are correspondingly limited to the legal architecture of liability rather than to its practical enforcement rates, which remain largely undocumented.</jats:p>\", \"URL\": \"https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7473639\", \"published\": {\"date-parts\": [[2026]]}}]", "excerpt_truncated": false, "source_sha256": "68678b3e63340cd78f02c39a56edf872bc332a520b86c8a05da3f0668c5b0d01", "verification_required": true, "topic_domain": "responsibility_formation", "evidence_role": "discovery", "host_tier": "discovery", "source_identity": null, "persistent_identifiers": ["doi:10.2139/ssrn.7483422", "doi:10.4324/9781315201399-4", "doi:10.1007/978-3-032-15112-4_18", "doi:10.2139/ssrn.7473639"], "source_candidates": ["https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7483422", "https://doi.org/10.4324/9781315201399-4", "https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-15112-4_18", "https://doi.org/10.2139/ssrn.7473639"], "source_candidate_identities": {}}
